item.title: Flip the Bottle: How to Buy Baijiu Without Getting Robbed
item.description: The four digits on the back label tell you what is actually in the bottle. How to read a baijiu standard number, what 100 to 300 yuan really buys, where to shop outside China, and how not to get robbed when the occasion calls for a gift.

item.title: The Rules of the Table: Why Your Glass Has to Sit Lower
item.description: A Chinese banquet is a ranking system with food on it. Who toasts whom, why your rim drops below theirs, what ganbei commits you to, and eight rules for surviving the evening.

item.title: The Half Bottle Problem: What Really Happens to Baijiu After You Open It
item.description: The clock starts when you twist the cap. What esters, oxygen and a growing headspace do to an opened bottle of baijiu, why 53 percent is not magic, and four rules that keep it drinkable.

item.title: The Switch Nobody Dated: How Shaojiu Took China From Huangjiu
item.description: China drank a 15 percent fermented wine for two thousand years, then quietly changed its national drink. The still, the crop, and a date nobody wrote down.

item.title: Daughter's Wine: The Jar Buried the Day She Was Born
item.description: In Shaoxing a family brews a jar of huangjiu the winter a daughter is born and digs it up at her wedding. What eighteen years underground do to the wine, and how to tell an aged bottle from a story with a red box.

item.title: Jade Ice Burn: The Baijiu That Ages With Pork Fat
item.description: In Foshan they distill rice spirit, drop a slab of pork fat into the jar and wait. Yuk Bing Siu is 29 percent alcohol, faintly savoury, and the only baijiu in China defined by what floats inside it.

item.title: Huangjiu 101: China's Oldest Alcohol, and Why the West Has Never Heard of It
item.description: Huangjiu is China's oldest alcohol: glutinous rice and wheat qu, fermented and never distilled, served warm in a bowl of hot water. Three thousand years of amber wine, why the great poems were written over it, and why it never crossed the ocean.

item.title: Chinese Alcohol 101: Where Baijiu, Huangjiu and Rice Wine Split Apart
item.description: Chinese alcohol all begins the same way: grain and qu, a mold starter. Then it splits. Ferment it and you get huangjiu and rice wine; distill it and you get baijiu. A map of the four families, and how to tell which bottle is in your hand.

item.title: Three Glasses, One Table: How to Actually Drink Baijiu
item.description: Moutai, Wuliangye and Guojiao 1573 side by side on one table. How to smell baijiu, where the burn comes from, what finish means, and what to eat with it.

item.title: The Pit That Never Stopped: 450 Years of Mud, and the Men Who Tend It
item.description: Four fermentation pits in Luzhou have been working since 1573. The mud in their walls is the recipe nobody can copy, and the men who tend it cannot be replaced.

item.title: Baijiu 101: The Four Aromas, and Why Chinese Sort Liquor the Way They Sort Tea
item.description: Every baijiu bottle is stamped with one of four aroma types. What sauce, strong, light and rice actually mean, how the spirit ferments as solid grain, and how to drink your first glass.

item.title: The Moutai Puzzle: Why a Bottle Costs More Than Your Graphics Card
item.description: China's most famous spirit — sauce-aroma baijiu from Guizhou's Chishui River, worth more than Diageo.
